They say in politics there are no permanent friends or enemies, but when a compliment comes from the most unexpected quarters, it can create more ripples than the fiercest political attack.
At a time

when Rahul Gandhi and the Congress party are leaving no stone unturned in their offensive against Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a voice from the very heart of the Gandhi family's inner circle has struck a remarkably different note.

Sam Petroda, Rajiv Gandhi's trusted advisor, a Gandhi family confidant for decades on end, Rahul Gandhi's loyal lieutenant and guru, and the man who heads the Indian Overseas Congress, the very man gearing up to coordinate Rahul Gandhi's upcoming US visit.
where the Congress leader is expected to renew his criticism of the Modi government at Columbia University no less.
He has now showered lavish praise on Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Not a grudging acknowledgement, not a passing compliment, but a glowing account of Modi's personal warmth, kindness, affection and leadership qualities.
And coming from one of Rahul Gandhi's most trusted men, the timing and the choice of words are particularly striking.
Don't believe us?
Well, listen in for yourselves.

And Prime Minister Narendra Modi was quick to reciprocate with a personal touch on social media platform X. Addressing Petroda as Sam Bhai and his wife as Anjana Ben, he wrote and I quote, Happy Diwali and New Year Abhinandan.
Praying for a joyful and healthy year ahead.
Jai Jagannath.
In fact, when a social media user cheekily asked, Sam Pitroda ko Diwali wish kar sakte hain, to humme bhi wish kar do, Modi ji.
And the Prime Minister promptly replied, aapko bhi Happy Diwali, Mihir Bhai.
And the warmth extended beyond social media.
At the BJP's Diwali Milan, Prime Minister Modi fondly recalled his decades-old association with journalists.

From political adversaries to old acquaintances, a reminder that political equations may change, ideological battles may intensify, but personal relationships and courtesies need not become casualties of political rivalry.
One day, a gang of journalists entered my room.
At that time, there was a women's brigade.

But here's the irony.
Sonia Gandhi in her newly released memoir has presented a strikingly different portrait of Narendra Modi.
She claims that despite over 12 years of his prime ministership, they have had practically no real conversation.
That when they come face to face, the prime minister offers a formal namaste but avoids eye contact.
But since when did political courtesy come with an obligation of personal attention?
Sonia Gandhi speaks of distance while her family's longtime confidant Sam Petroda speaks of warmth, affection and mutual respect.
And if that contrast wasn't striking enough, Petroda's praise has now sparked a backlash within the opposition itself with a Congress leader who's even speculating about his political loyalty.
We don't live in this country, so we don't know what's going on there.
That's why they must have said that they are thinking of killing us.
This is what even alliance partners are talking about Sam Petroda, a man so close to Mr Rahul Gandhi's heart.
But this is hardly the first time Prime Minister Narendra Modi has demonstrated that political differences need not come in the way of personal courtesies.
Remember his warm interaction with former Prime Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh at the inauguration of the Kartarpur Sahib corridor.
Two political adversaries sharing a cordial moment despite years of ideological differences.
honoring the position of a former prime minister or that emotional farewell to congress veteran Ghulam Nabi Azad in parliament itself.
Modi broke down, wiped his tears and saluted Azad recalling their decades-old association when Gujarati
Citizens had been affected by floods and Ghulam Nabi Azad as a Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir had helped out.
Then there was that small but telling gesture towards Sharad Pawar.
The Prime Minister helped the veteran leader with his chair and poured water for him.
A simple act of courtesy despite their political differences.
And even with Rahul Gandhi, his fiercest political rival, Modi has shared moments of cordiality.

Remember their candid interaction at Prerna's Thal in Parliament, when they shared a lighter moment away from the political battlefield, and after Operation Sindoor when the Prime Minister reached out to leaders across party lines, meeting members of all party delegations who had taken India's message against terrorism to the world,
Political differences set aside in national interest and perhaps the Prime Minister himself summed up this approach best when he reflected on 25 years in public life.
Whoever made me win, taught me to be humble.
Whoever made me fall, taught me
Then I was taught to stand.
The good thinkers encouraged me.
And the bad thinkers taught me to look inside myself.
Now let's take a look at the other side of this debate on political courtesies.
The BJP has repeatedly pointed to the Congress's own record of bitter, often deeply personal attacks on the Prime Minister.
From Rahul Gandhi's Chaukidar Chor Hai campaign to Malik Arjun Kharges, Modi Ka Baap Bhi Jai Ka remark and the controversial, Modi Teri Kabr Khudegi, slogans raised at Congress protests.
Here's a glimpse of the muhabbat
showered on the Prime Minister by the Congress party and the Gandhi family.

When even Rahul Gandhi's most trusted loyalist has words of admiration and praise for Narendra Modi's personal warmth, kindness and character, is there a lesson for the Congress party?
Well, that's the question.
That's the debate on the other side.
You're watching the news hour at night.
Debate number one on Times Now.
Super Prime Time.
